notes.front: What is an installment agreement?
notes.back: A monthly payment plan agreed with the IRS by a taxpayer who cannot pay the full amount owed.
notes.explanation: The Form 9465 instructions describe it as the monthly payment plan a taxpayer asks for when the full amount on the return or notice cannot be paid.
notes.example: Like buying a car on monthly terms, but the lender is the IRS and the debt is a tax bill.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 9465 (Rev. July 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Form 9465 to request a monthly installment agreement (payment plan) if you can’t pay the full amount

notes.front: What is a guaranteed installment agreement?
notes.back: An installment agreement the IRS must accept for an individual’s income tax when the conditions of section 6159(c) are met.
notes.explanation: Section 6159(c) says the Secretary “shall” enter into the agreement when its conditions hold, so the IRS has no discretion to refuse it.
notes.example: Like a shop that must honour a layaway plan for any small purchase that meets its printed rules, rather than deciding case by case.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6159, Agreements for payment of tax liability in installments, “(c) Secretary required to enter into installment agreements in certain cases”
notes.evidence: the Secretary shall enter into an agreement to accept the full payment of such tax in installments if, as of the date the individual offers to enter into the agreement

notes.front: What is an offer in compromise (OIC)?
notes.back: An agreement between the taxpayer and the IRS that settles a tax debt for less than the full amount owed.
notes.explanation: The Form 656 Booklet defines the offer this way and says it is generally based on what the IRS considers the taxpayer’s ability to pay.
notes.example: Like a creditor agreeing to take part of a debt as full settlement, but the creditor is the IRS and it weighs your ability to pay.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “What is an Offer?”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An Offer in Compromise (offer) is an agreement between you (the taxpayer) and the IRS that settles a tax debt for less than the full amount owed.

notes.front: What is doubt as to collectibility?
notes.back: An offer ground: the taxpayer does not have enough assets and income to pay the full tax liability.
notes.explanation: On Form 656 the taxpayer ticking this box states that assets and income fall short and that the minimum offer from the collection information statement has been offered.
notes.example: Like a debtor showing the lender that everything they own and earn will never cover the balance.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Form 656, Section 3, Reason for Offer”, p. 25
notes.evidence: Doubt as to Collectibility - I do not have enough in assets and income to pay my full tax liability.

notes.front: What is doubt as to liability?
notes.back: An offer ground: a legitimate doubt that the taxpayer owes part or all of the tax debt. It uses Form 656-L.
notes.explanation: The booklet sends taxpayers who genuinely doubt that the tax is owed to Form 656-L rather than Form 656.
notes.example: Like disputing a bill because you think the charge itself is wrong, not because you cannot afford it.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Doubt as to Liability”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you have a legitimate doubt that you owe part or all of the tax debt, complete and submit a Form 656-L, Offer in Compromise (Doubt as to Liability).

notes.front: What is effective tax administration as an offer ground?
notes.back: The taxpayer owes the tax and could pay in full, but special circumstances make full payment an economic hardship or unfair.
notes.explanation: Form 656 offers two effective tax administration boxes: economic hardship, and public policy or equity. Both start from the admission that the tax is owed and payable.
notes.example: Like a lender easing a debt the borrower could technically pay, because collecting it all would cause serious hardship.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Form 656, Section 3, Reason for Offer”, p. 25
notes.evidence: Effective Tax Administration - Economic Hardship - I owe this tax liability and have enough in assets and income to pay my liability in full.

notes.front: What is currently not collectible (CNC) status?
notes.back: An account status, given for financial hardship, in which the IRS temporarily suspends most collection activity.
notes.explanation: The IRS page says it may place the account in CNC status when the taxpayer cannot pay because of financial hardship, delaying collection until things improve.
notes.example: Like a landlord agreeing to stop chasing rent arrears for now because the tenant has lost their job, while the arrears stay on the books.
notes.source: IRS, “Temporarily delay the collection process”, “How it works”
notes.evidence: we may place your account in Currently Not Collectible (CNC) status, which means: We have temporarily suspended most collection activities.

notes.front: What is a federal tax lien?
notes.back: The government’s legal claim against all of a taxpayer’s current and future property for an unpaid tax debt.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the lien is created by law when the first bill goes unpaid and attaches to property and rights to property.
notes.example: Like a mortgage lender’s charge over a house, but it arises automatically and covers everything the taxpayer owns or later acquires.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Federal Tax Lien: A legal claim against property”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A lien is a legal claim against all your current and future property.

notes.front: What is a Notice of Federal Tax Lien (NFTL)?
notes.back: A public filing that tells creditors about the tax debt and establishes the IRS’s priority against certain other creditors.
notes.explanation: The booklet separates the lien itself, which arises by law, from the NFTL, which the IRS files to give public notice and secure priority.
notes.example: Like registering a charge at the land registry: the debt already existed, but now other lenders can see it.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Notice of Federal Tax Lien”, p. 4
notes.evidence: A Notice of Federal Tax Lien (NFTL) provides public notice of the tax debt to creditors. The IRS files the NFTL to establish priority of the IRS claim versus the claims of certain other creditors.

notes.front: What is a certificate of release of federal tax lien?
notes.back: A document the IRS issues, for filing where the NFTL was recorded, once all liabilities on the notice are satisfied.
notes.explanation: Publication 1450 says the certificate is filed in the same recording office as the original notice, so the public record shows the lien is gone.
notes.example: Like the lender’s letter confirming a loan is paid off, lodged at the same registry where the charge was recorded.
notes.source: Publication 1450, Instructions for Requesting a Certificate of Release of Federal Tax Lien (Rev. 7-2018), “Instructions for Requesting a Certificate of Release of Federal Tax Lien”, p. 1
notes.evidence: When all the liabilities shown on the Notice of Federal Tax Lien are satisfied, we will issue a Certificate of Release of Federal Tax Lien for filing in the same recording office where the notice of lien was filed.

notes.front: What does a certificate of discharge do?
notes.back: It removes a specific piece of property from the federal tax lien; the lien stays on everything else.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says a discharge removes specific property from the lien, and points to Publication 783 for how to qualify.
notes.example: Like a lender freeing one field from a farm mortgage so it can be sold, while the rest of the farm stays mortgaged.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “How to apply for a “discharge” of a Federal Tax Lien from property”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A “discharge” removes specific property from the federal tax lein.

notes.front: What is subordination of a federal tax lien?
notes.back: Letting another creditor move ahead of the government’s priority position; the lien itself stays in place.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 describes subordination as making the federal tax lien secondary to another creditor, and refers to Publication 784 for eligibility.
notes.example: Like a first lender agreeing to stand behind a new lender in the queue so that a loan can go ahead.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “How to make the Federal Tax Lien secondary to other creditors (“subordination”)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A “subordination” is where a creditor is allowed to move ahead of

notes.front: What is a levy?
notes.back: The legal taking of a taxpayer’s property or rights to property to collect unpaid tax.
notes.explanation: Section 6331(a) lets the IRS collect unpaid tax by levy on all property and rights to property, except exempt property.
notes.example: Like a bailiff taking goods to pay a court debt, but done by the IRS for tax, and it can reach wages and bank balances too.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6331, Levy and distraint, “(a) Authority of Secretary”
notes.evidence: it shall be lawful for the Secretary to collect such tax (and such further sum as shall be sufficient to cover the expenses of the levy) by levy upon all property and rights to property

notes.front: In IRS collection, what is a seizure?
notes.back: The IRS taking property to satisfy a tax debt. Publication 594 says there is no legal difference between a seizure and a levy.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 uses the two words interchangeably for the same collection action.
notes.example: Like a levy on a bank account, but the word is often used when the IRS takes physical property such as a car and sells it.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Levy: A seizure of property”, p. 5
notes.evidence: There is no legal difference between a seizure and a levy.

notes.front: What is a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing?
notes.back: An appeal hearing, available by law after certain lien and levy notices, in which Appeals reviews the collection action.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 lists the notices that open a CDP hearing, including the lien-filing notice and the final notice of intent to levy.
notes.example: Like a statutory right to have an independent reviewer look at a bailiff’s action, triggered by a specific warning letter.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “Collection Due Process”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Collection Due Process (CDP) is available if you receive one of the following notices:

notes.front: What is an equivalent hearing (EH)?
notes.back: A hearing like a CDP hearing, given when the request does not meet the requirements for a timely CDP hearing.
notes.explanation: Form 12153 asks for an equivalent hearing through a box used when the CDP request is not timely.
notes.example: Like a late appeal the reviewer agrees to hear, but without the full rights that a timely appeal carries.
notes.source: Form 12153, Request for a Collection Due Process or Equivalent Hearing (July 2022), “Line 2, Equivalent Hearing”, p. 1
notes.evidence: If my request does not meet the requirements for a timely CDP hearing, I would like a hearing that is equivalent to a CDP hearing

notes.front: What is the Collection Appeals Program (CAP)?
notes.back: An Appeals procedure for a broad range of collection actions that usually gives a quicker decision than CDP.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 describes CAP as quicker and broader than CDP, and says CAP covers liens, levies, seizures and installment agreement decisions.
notes.example: Like asking a manager’s manager to overrule a decision quickly, without the option of going on to court.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “Collection Appeals Program”, p. 1
notes.evidence: CAP generally results in a quicker Appeals decision and is available for a broader range of collection actions.

notes.front: What is a refund offset?
notes.back: Using all or part of a taxpayer’s overpayment to pay certain past-due debts instead of refunding it.
notes.explanation: The Form 1040 instructions say an overpayment may be used to pay past-due federal tax and certain other debts.
notes.example: Like an employer deducting an outstanding staff loan from a bonus before paying the rest.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 (2025), “Refund Offset”, p. 61
notes.evidence: all or part of the overpayment on line 34 may be used (offset) to pay the past-due amount.

notes.front: What is an abatement in IRS terms?
notes.back: A reduction or removal of an assessed tax, penalty, addition to tax, interest or fee.
notes.explanation: Form 843 is used to claim a refund or request an abatement of certain taxes, penalties, additions to tax, interest and fees.
notes.example: Like a council cancelling part of a charge it has already billed, instead of refunding money you have not yet paid.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 843 (Rev. December 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Form 843 to claim a refund or request an abatement of certain taxes, penalties, additions to tax, interest, and fees.

notes.front: What is audit reconsideration?
notes.back: An IRS process to re-examine an audit result (or an IRS-prepared return) that the taxpayer disagrees with.
notes.explanation: Publication 3598 says the process helps when you disagree with the results of an IRS audit of your return, or of a return created by the IRS because you did not file.
notes.example: Like asking a marker to look again at an exam after the result is out, because you now have the working you failed to hand in.
notes.source: Publication 3598, The Audit Reconsideration Process (Rev. 11-2023), “What is Audit Reconsideration?”, p. 1
notes.evidence: disagree with the results of an IRS audit of your tax

notes.front: What is an IRS summons?
notes.back: A legal order that compels the taxpayer or a third party to meet an IRS officer and give information, documents or testimony.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the IRS may serve a summons when it has trouble gathering information to determine or collect tax.
notes.example: Like a witness summons from a court, but issued by the IRS to get records or testimony.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Summons: Used to secure information”, p. 7
notes.evidence: A summons legally compels you or a third party to meet with an officer of the IRS and

notes.front: What is the trust fund recovery penalty (TFRP)?
notes.back: A penalty assessed personally against those responsible for paying over withheld trust fund taxes who wilfully did not do so.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 describes the TFRP as assessed personally against the responsible individuals, which is why it can follow a person after the business fails.
notes.example: Like making a company director personally pay money the company held for someone else and spent.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Trust Fund Recovery Penalty”, p. 8
notes.evidence: personally against the individual or individuals who were responsible for paying the trust fund taxes, but who willfully did not do so.

notes.front: Who can be a responsible person for the TFRP?
notes.back: Anyone responsible for collecting, accounting for or paying over trust fund taxes: an officer or employee, among others.
notes.explanation: Publication 15 lists officers and employees of a corporation, partners, accountants, volunteer directors and others; the test is responsibility, not job title.
notes.example: Like a treasurer who signs the cheques and decides which bills to pay, whatever their formal title.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2026), Employer's Tax Guide, “Trust fund recovery penalty”, p. 36
notes.evidence: A responsible person can be an officer or employee

notes.front: What is a seriously delinquent tax debt?
notes.back: A legally enforceable, unpaid federal tax debt above an inflation-adjusted threshold that the IRS may certify to the State Department.
notes.explanation: The IRS page defines it by amount (adjusted yearly) and by collection status, and certification can lead to passport denial or revocation.
notes.example: Like a large unpaid court debt that gets you flagged at the border, but here the flag goes to the passport office.
notes.source: IRS, “Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes”, “What are seriously delinquent tax debts?”
notes.evidence: Seriously delinquent tax debts are legally enforceable, unpaid federal tax debt (including assessed penalties and interest)

notes.front: What does the IRS send first when a filed return shows tax owed?
notes.back: A bill for the tax due, calculated from the return, plus any interest and penalties.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 calls this the first bill for the tax due in its general steps from billing to collection.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “General steps from billing to collection”, p. 2
notes.evidence: If you owe taxes, we will send you a bill. This is your first bill for

notes.front: A client ignored the IRS’s first bill and a reminder, and has now received a final bill that he also cannot pay. What comes next if he does nothing?
notes.back: B: the IRS begins collection actions.
notes.choices:
A) The IRS must first reassess the tax
B) The IRS begins collection actions
C) Nothing until the debt is two years old
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: no new assessment is needed for billed tax. C is wrong: Publication 594 sets no such waiting period.
notes.explanation: In Publication 594’s third step, an unpaid final bill leads to collection actions, from refund offsets to seizure.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “General steps from billing to collection”, p. 2
notes.evidence: If you still don’t pay after you receive your final bill, we will

notes.front: Under section 6331(a), levy becomes lawful if the taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay within {{c1::10 days}} after notice and demand.
notes.back: 10 days.
notes.explanation: Section 6331(a) ties the levy power to non-payment within 10 days of notice and demand; the separate 30-day notice of intent in 6331(d) must also be given.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6331, Levy and distraint, “(a) Authority of Secretary”
notes.evidence: If any person liable to pay any tax neglects or refuses to pay the same within 10 days after notice and demand, it shall be lawful for the Secretary to collect such tax

notes.front: Who may represent a taxpayer during the collection process?
notes.back: The taxpayer, or an attorney, certified public accountant, enrolled agent, immediate family member or other person enrolled to practise before the IRS.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 lists these representatives and adds that a business may also be represented by full-time employees, general partners or bona fide officers.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Representation during the collection process”, p. 8
notes.evidence: represented by yourself, an attorney, a certified public accountant, an enrolled agent, an immediate family member, or any person enrolled

notes.front: What must a Form 1127 applicant show to prove undue hardship?
notes.back: That paying on the due date would cause a substantial financial loss, such as selling property at a sacrifice price.
notes.explanation: The form gives the forced sale of property at a sacrifice price as its example of such a loss.
notes.source: Form 1127, Application for Extension of Time for Payment of Tax Due to Undue Hardship (Rev. December 2024), “Purpose of Form: Undue hardship”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You must show you will have a substantial financial loss (such as selling property at a sacrifice price) if you pay your tax

notes.front: By when must Form 1127 be received to extend payment of tax shown on a return?
notes.back: On or before the return’s due date, not counting extensions.
notes.explanation: Form 1127 says an extension to file does not move this deadline; for a deficiency the deadline is the payment date in the bill instead.
notes.source: Form 1127, Application for Extension of Time for Payment of Tax Due to Undue Hardship (Rev. December 2024), “When To File”, p. 3
notes.evidence: 1127 must be received on or before the due date of that return, not including extensions.

notes.front: An extension to pay tax shown on a return is generally not granted for more than {{c1::6 months}}, unless the taxpayer is out of the country.
notes.back: 6 months.
notes.explanation: Form 1127 allows a longer extension for a taxpayer out of the country, except for certain excise taxes.
notes.source: Form 1127, Application for Extension of Time for Payment of Tax Due to Undue Hardship (Rev. December 2024), “Extension Period”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An extension of more than 6 months will generally not be granted

notes.front: A client can pay her tax due on 15 April only by selling a rental flat quickly at well below its value. She would repay in full in four months. What should you consider first?
notes.back: C: Form 1127, extension of time to pay for undue hardship, received by the return’s due date.
notes.choices:
A) Form 1127 filed after the due date with an extension to file
B) An offer in compromise
C) Form 1127, extension of time to pay for undue hardship
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: she can pay in full, just not on the due date. C is wrong: Form 1127 must be received by the due date, and an extension to file does not extend that.
notes.explanation: Selling property at a sacrifice price is the form’s own example of the substantial financial loss that proves undue hardship.
notes.source: Form 1127, Application for Extension of Time for Payment of Tax Due to Undue Hardship (Rev. December 2024), “Purpose of Form: Undue hardship”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You must show you will have a substantial financial loss (such as selling property at a sacrifice price) if you pay your tax

notes.front: Under the Form 9465 instructions (Rev. July 2024), up to what balance can a taxpayer apply online for a payment plan instead of filing Form 9465?
notes.explanation: The Form 9465 instructions add that the online application carries a lower user fee.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 9465 (Rev. July 2024), “Applying online for an installment agreement and other payment plans”, p. 1
notes.evidence: If your balance due isn’t more than $50,000, you can apply online for a payment plan

notes.front: Under the Form 9465 instructions (Rev. July 2024), what assessed liability generally qualifies an individual for a streamlined installment agreement without special payment conditions?
notes.back: $25,000 or less.
notes.explanation: The instructions extend streamlined treatment to $25,001–$50,000 for an individual who agrees to direct debit or payroll deduction.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 9465 (Rev. July 2024), “Streamlined installment agreement”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Your assessed tax liability is $25,000 or less

notes.front: A client asks for an installment agreement for 2024 tax but has not filed her 2023 return. What must happen first?
notes.back: C: she must file all required returns, including 2023.
notes.choices:
A) Pay the user fee in advance
B) Nothing: only the 2024 year matters
C) File all required returns, including 2023
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: eligibility needs all required returns filed. C is wrong: the user fee can come out of the first payments.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 makes filing all required returns a condition of a payment plan.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Apply for a Payment Plan (Installment Agreement)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: To be eligible for a payment plan, you must file all required tax returns.

notes.front: For an individual who filed on time, at what monthly rate does the late payment penalty accrue while an installment agreement is in effect?
notes.back: 0.25% a month, instead of up to 1% a month.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 describes the lower rate as a reduction that applies while the installment agreement is in effect.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Apply for a Payment Plan (Installment Agreement)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: The late payment penalty accrues at the rate of 0.25% per month, instead of up to 1% per month.

notes.front: Can the IRS issue a new levy while an installment agreement request is pending?
notes.back: No. It cannot issue a new levy during a current or pending payment plan or offer in compromise.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 adds economic hardship, where levy would leave the taxpayer unable to meet basic living expenses, to the same list.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Levy: A seizure of property”, p. 6
notes.evidence: We can’t issue a new levy if you have a current or pending payment

notes.front: Under the fees in effect from 1 July 2024, what is the user fee for a direct debit installment agreement set up online, and one set up another way?
notes.back: $22 online; $107 not using the online application.
notes.explanation: The Form 9465 instructions show the direct debit row of the fee table; paying by cheque or card costs more ($69 or $178).
notes.source: Instructions for Form 9465 (Rev. July 2024), “Installment agreement user fees”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Direct debit $22* $107*

notes.front: Under section 6159(c), as in force for 2025, what is the maximum liability for a guaranteed installment agreement?
notes.back: $10,000, not counting interest, penalties, additions to tax and additional amounts.
notes.explanation: Section 6159(c)(1) measures the $10,000 limit without interest and penalties.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6159, Agreements for payment of tax liability in installments, “(c) Secretary required to enter into installment agreements in certain cases”
notes.evidence: the aggregate amount of such liability (determined without regard to interest, penalties, additions to the tax, and additional amounts) does not exceed $10,000;

notes.front: Over how many preceding tax years must a taxpayer have a clean filing and payment record for a guaranteed installment agreement?
notes.back: 5 years: no failure to file, no failure to pay and no income tax installment agreement.
notes.explanation: Section 6159(c)(2) applies the test to the spouse too when the liability is on a joint return.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6159, Agreements for payment of tax liability in installments, “(c) Secretary required to enter into installment agreements in certain cases”
notes.evidence: has not, during any of the preceding 5 taxable years- (A) failed to file any return of tax imposed by subtitle A;

notes.front: A client owes $8,500 of income tax (before interest and penalties) and cannot pay it when due. For the last five years he filed and paid on time and never had a payment plan. Must the IRS accept his three-year installment agreement?
notes.back: A: yes. It is a guaranteed installment agreement.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it is a guaranteed installment agreement
B) No, the IRS always has discretion
C) Only if he owes more than $10,000
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: section 6159(c) says the Secretary “shall” enter into the agreement when its conditions are met. C reverses the rule: the limit is $10,000 or less.
notes.explanation: He is under the $10,000 limit in section 6159(c) as in force for 2025, has the clean five-year record, cannot pay in full when due and will pay within three years.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6159, Agreements for payment of tax liability in installments, “(c) Secretary required to enter into installment agreements in certain cases”
notes.evidence: the Secretary shall enter into an agreement to accept the full payment of such tax in installments if

notes.front: A client owes $42,000 in total and wants a payment plan at the lowest user fee. What do you advise?
notes.back: B: apply online through the Online Payment Agreement application.
notes.choices:
A) Request a guaranteed installment agreement
B) Apply online through the Online Payment Agreement application
C) File Form 1127
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a guaranteed installment agreement needs $10,000 or less (section 6159(c), 2025). C is wrong: Form 1127 is an extension of time to pay for undue hardship, not a payment plan.
notes.explanation: The balance is within the $50,000 online limit in the Form 9465 instructions (Rev. July 2024), and the online route carries a lower user fee.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 9465 (Rev. July 2024), “Applying online for an installment agreement and other payment plans”, p. 1
notes.evidence: the user fee that you pay will be lower than it would be otherwise.

notes.front: A client wants to submit an offer in compromise. He has filed every return but has not received a bill for any debt in the offer. What should you advise?
notes.back: B: wait until he has a bill for at least one of the debts.
notes.choices:
A) Submit now: filing is the only condition
B) Wait until he receives a bill for at least one debt
C) Submit Form 656-L instead
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a bill for at least one debt is also required. C is wrong: he does not dispute the liability.
notes.explanation: The booklet lists receiving a bill for at least one included debt among the conditions for consideration.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Are You Eligible?”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Before your offer can be considered, you must (1) file all tax returns you are legally required to file, (2) have received a bill for at least one tax debt included on your offer,

notes.front: Will the IRS generally accept an offer from a taxpayer who could pay in full through an installment agreement or equity in assets?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The booklet points such taxpayers to effective tax administration only if full payment would cause economic hardship or be unjust.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Can You Pay in Full?”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Generally, the IRS will not accept an offer if you can pay your tax debt in full through an installment agreement and/or equity in assets.

notes.front: May a taxpayer submit a doubt as to liability offer and a doubt as to collectibility offer at the same time?
notes.back: No. Resolve the doubt about liability first, then offer on ability to pay.
notes.explanation: The booklet says any doubt about owing the debt must be settled before an offer based on ability to pay.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Doubt as to Liability”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Do not submit both an offer under Doubt as to Liability and an offer under Doubt as to Collectibility or Effective Tax Administration at the same time.

notes.front: Who can qualify for an effective tax administration offer on economic hardship grounds?
notes.back: Only individuals.
notes.explanation: Form 656 limits the economic hardship box to individuals; the public policy or equity box has no such limit on its face.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Form 656, Section 3, Reason for Offer”, p. 25
notes.evidence: requiring full payment would cause an economic hardship. (Only individuals qualify for this consideration).

notes.front: What application fee does the April 2026 Form 656 Booklet require with an offer in compromise?
notes.back: $205, unless the individual meets the Low-Income Certification guidelines.
notes.explanation: Each Form 656 needs its own fee, so a joint and a separate offer, or an individual and a business offer, each pay it.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Application Fee”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Offers require a $205 application fee.

notes.front: What does an individual who meets the Low-Income Certification guidelines not have to send with an offer?
notes.back: The application fee and any offer payments, on submission or while the offer is considered.
notes.explanation: The booklet treats someone as an individual when compromising a personal liability, including one incurred as a sole proprietor.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Application Fee”, p. 5
notes.evidence: If you are an individual and meet the Low-Income Certification guidelines, there is no requirement to submit any offer payments or the application fee

notes.front: What must accompany a lump-sum offer, and how is the rest paid?
notes.back: 20% of the total offer with the application; the balance in 5 or fewer payments within 5 months of acceptance.
notes.explanation: The booklet defines the lump-sum option by these two limits.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Payment Options”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Lump Sum: This option requires 20% of the total offer amount to be paid with the offer and the remaining balance paid in 5 or fewer payments within 5 or fewer months of the date your offer is accepted.

notes.front: Under the periodic payment option, over what period is the balance of the offer paid?
notes.back: In monthly payments within 6 to 24 months, after a first payment sent with the offer.
notes.explanation: The taxpayer must also keep making the monthly payments while the IRS evaluates the offer.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Payment Options”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Periodic Payment: This option requires you to make the first payment with the offer and the remaining balance paid in monthly payments within 6 to 24 months

notes.front: A client’s periodic payment offer is under review. He misses two monthly payments before any decision. What may the IRS do, and can he appeal?
notes.back: B: the IRS may return the offer, and he cannot appeal that.
notes.choices:
A) Reject the offer, with appeal rights
B) Return the offer, with no appeal
C) Nothing until the offer is decided
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: missed payments lead to return, which cannot be appealed. C is wrong: payments must continue during the evaluation.
notes.explanation: The booklet says missing periodic payments before a final decision may lead to the offer being returned.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Payment Options”, p. 5
notes.evidence: If you fail to make these payments at any time prior to receiving a final decision letter, the IRS may return your offer. You cannot appeal this decision.

notes.front: After an offer is accepted, for how long must the taxpayer stay current with filing and payment?
notes.back: Through the fifth year after acceptance.
notes.explanation: The booklet warns that failing to stay current in this period may lead the IRS to default the offer.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Other Important Facts”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If the IRS accepts your offer, you must continue to stay current with all tax filing and payment obligations through the fifth year after your offer is accepted.

notes.front: What is the difference in appeal rights between a rejected offer and a returned offer?
notes.back: A rejected offer can be appealed; a returned offer cannot.
notes.explanation: The booklet states both rules side by side; offers returned for missed payments or unfiled returns carry no appeal.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Other Important Facts”, p. 4
notes.evidence: You have the right to appeal if the IRS rejects your offer. You do not have the right to appeal if the IRS returns your offer.

notes.front: What happens to a refund on a return assessed before the IRS accepts an offer?
notes.back: The IRS may keep it, with interest, by offsetting it against the tax debt; it does not count as an offer payment.
notes.explanation: The booklet says the offset refund reduces the outstanding liability rather than paying towards the offer amount.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Your Tax Refunds”, p. 3
notes.evidence: The IRS may keep any tax refund, including interest, for a tax return assessed before the date the IRS accepts your offer by offsetting it against your tax debt

notes.front: A client mailed an offer in compromise last week. Before the IRS acknowledged it as pending, the IRS levied his bank account. Can the IRS keep the money?
notes.back: C: yes. The IRS may levy until the offer is signed as pending and may keep the proceeds.
notes.choices:
A) No, the levy must be returned once the offer is accepted
B) No, mailing the offer stops all levies
C) Yes, it may keep the proceeds
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: protection starts when the IRS official acknowledges the offer as pending. C is wrong: the booklet says the IRS may keep levy proceeds.
notes.explanation: The booklet allows levy up to the time the offer is acknowledged as pending.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “What you need to know”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The IRS may levy your assets up to the time the IRS official signs and acknowledges your offer as pending.

notes.front: A corporation owes unpaid payroll taxes, including trust fund taxes, and wants to submit an offer. No TFRP determinations have been made. Can its offer be considered now?
notes.back: C: no, not until the trust fund portion is paid or the TFRP determinations are made.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if it offers 20% down
B) Yes, any business may submit an offer
C) No, not until the trust fund part is paid or TFRP determinations are made
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the booklet bars such businesses. C is wrong: the payment option does not cure the bar.
notes.explanation: The booklet makes trust fund payment or TFRP determinations a precondition, except for victims of payroll service provider fraud.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Trust Fund Taxes”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Your business is not eligible for consideration of an offer unless the trust fund portion of the tax is paid or the IRS has made the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty determination(s) on all potentially responsible parties.

notes.front: A retired client agrees she owes $60,000 but has only a small pension and no assets of value, so the debt will never be paid. Which offer ground fits?
notes.back: C: doubt as to collectibility.
notes.choices:
A) Effective tax administration
B) Doubt as to liability
C) Doubt as to collectibility
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: she accepts that she owes the tax. C is wrong: that ground starts from having enough to pay in full.
notes.explanation: Her assets and income are not enough to pay the full liability, which is the collectibility ground.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Form 656, Section 3, Reason for Offer”, p. 25
notes.evidence: Doubt as to Collectibility - I do not have enough in assets and income to pay my full tax liability.

notes.front: A client has savings to pay a $15,000 assessment but has a genuine basis for believing most of it was assessed in error. Which offer ground and form fit?
notes.back: B: doubt as to liability, on Form 656-L.
notes.choices:
A) Doubt as to collectibility, on Form 656
B) Doubt as to liability, on Form 656-L
C) Effective tax administration, on Form 656
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: he can pay. C is wrong: effective tax administration begins by accepting that the tax is owed.
notes.explanation: A legitimate doubt that the debt is owed points to Form 656-L.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Doubt as to Liability”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you have a legitimate doubt that you owe part or all of the tax debt, complete and submit a Form 656-L, Offer in Compromise (Doubt as to Liability).

notes.front: A client owes tax she accepts and has enough equity in her home to pay it, but she is seriously ill and paying would leave her unable to meet basic needs. Which offer ground fits?
notes.back: A: effective tax administration (economic hardship).
notes.choices:
A) Effective tax administration (economic hardship)
B) Doubt as to collectibility
C) Doubt as to liability
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: she has enough assets to pay. C is wrong: she accepts the liability.
notes.explanation: Economic hardship under effective tax administration starts from owing the tax and being able to pay it.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Form 656, Section 3, Reason for Offer”, p. 25
notes.evidence: Due to my special circumstances, requiring full payment would cause an economic hardship.

notes.front: A client (not low-income) offers $30,000 as a lump sum. How much must go with the Form 656, besides the application fee?
notes.back: C: $6,000 (20% of the offer).
notes.choices:
A) Nothing until the offer is accepted
B) $30,000
C) $6,000
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the rest can be paid in up to 5 payments after acceptance. C is wrong: only a low-income certified individual sends nothing.
notes.explanation: The lump-sum option needs 20% with the offer, and 20% of $30,000 is $6,000.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Payment Options”, p. 5
notes.evidence: This option requires 20% of the total offer amount to be paid with the offer

notes.front: A sole proprietor meets the Low-Income Certification guidelines and offers $4,000 on a personal liability. What must she send with Form 656?
notes.back: B: no fee and no offer payment.
notes.choices:
A) The $205 fee only
B) No fee and no offer payment
C) The $205 fee and 20% of the offer
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: low-income certification waives both the $205 fee (April 2026 booklet) and the payments during consideration.
notes.explanation: Liability incurred as a sole proprietor counts as individual, so the low-income waiver applies.
notes.source: Form 656 Booklet, Offer in Compromise (April 2026), “Application Fee”, p. 5
notes.evidence: You are considered an individual if you are seeking compromise of a liability for which you are personally responsible, including any liability you incurred as a sole proprietor.

notes.front: Does currently not collectible status cancel the tax debt?
notes.back: No. The taxpayer still owes the full amount; it is not forgiven or cancelled.
notes.explanation: The IRS page says only that most collection is suspended for the time being.
notes.source: IRS, “Temporarily delay the collection process”, “How it works”
notes.evidence: You still owe the full amount of your tax debt. It is not forgiven or cancelled.

notes.front: In CNC status, do penalties and interest keep accruing?
notes.back: Yes, until the balance is paid in full.
notes.explanation: The IRS page repeats this in its answers to frequently asked questions.
notes.source: IRS, “Temporarily delay the collection process”, “How it works”
notes.evidence: Penalties and interest continue to accrue until you pay your balance in full.

notes.front: Can the IRS file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien on an account in CNC status?
notes.back: Yes, to protect the government’s interest in the taxpayer’s property.
notes.explanation: The IRS page lists a lien filing among the things that may happen while in CNC status.
notes.source: IRS, “Temporarily delay the collection process”, “While in CNC status”
notes.evidence: We may file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien to protect the government’s interest in your property.

notes.front: How long does CNC status last?
notes.back: There is no fixed period; the IRS may review the taxpayer’s finances periodically.
notes.explanation: The IRS page says collection may resume if the ability to pay improves.
notes.source: IRS, “Temporarily delay the collection process”, “Frequently asked questions”
notes.evidence: There is no fixed time period. We may review your financial condition periodically to determine whether you can make payments.

notes.front: A client’s account went into CNC status last year. She has now filed a return showing a $1,200 refund. What will happen to it?
notes.back: C: the IRS will apply it to her unpaid tax debt.
notes.choices:
A) It is held until CNC status ends
B) She receives it because collection is suspended
C) The IRS will apply it to her unpaid tax debt
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: CNC suspends most collection, not refund offset. C is wrong: the IRS page says the refund is applied to the debt.
notes.explanation: The IRS page answers this question directly in its frequently asked questions.
notes.source: IRS, “Temporarily delay the collection process”, “Frequently asked questions”
notes.evidence: If you are due a federal tax refund, then we will apply it to your unpaid tax debt.

notes.front: A client owes assessed tax that he has not paid after the IRS’s demand. Six months later he inherits a house. Does the federal tax lien reach the house?
notes.back: A: yes. The lien covers all his property and rights to property, including property acquired later.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the lien reaches later-acquired property
B) No, only property owned when the tax was assessed
C) Only once a Notice of Federal Tax Lien is filed
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the lien attaches to current and future property. C is wrong: the lien arises by law; the notice gives public notice and priority.
notes.explanation: Section 6321 attaches the lien to all property and rights to property, and Publication 594 says this includes future property.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6321, Lien for taxes, “§ 6321”
notes.evidence: shall be a lien in favor of the United States upon all property and rights to property, whether real or personal, belonging to such person.

notes.front: Within how many business days of filing a Notice of Federal Tax Lien must the IRS notify the taxpayer?
notes.back: Not more than 5 business days after the filing.
notes.explanation: Section 6320 requires this written notice, which starts the CDP hearing clock.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6320, Notice and opportunity for hearing upon filing of notice of lien, “(a)(2) Time and method for notice”
notes.evidence: not more than 5 business days after the day of the filing of the notice of lien.

notes.front: The IRS filed a Notice of Federal Tax Lien against a client and mailed the notice three business days later. When does her 30-day window to request a CDP hearing start?
notes.back: C: the day after the 5-business-day notice period ends.
notes.choices:
A) The day the lien was filed
B) The day the notice was mailed
C) The day after the 5-business-day period ends
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: section 6320 starts the 30 days after the 5-day notice period, whatever day the notice went out.
notes.explanation: Section 6320 fixes the hearing window by reference to the five-day notice period.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6320, Notice and opportunity for hearing upon filing of notice of lien, “(a)(3) Information included with notice”
notes.evidence: the right of the person to request a hearing during the 30-day period beginning on the day after the 5-day period described in paragraph (2);

notes.front: A client paid his whole tax debt on 1 March. By about when must the IRS release the federal tax lien?
notes.back: C: within 30 days of full payment, by about 31 March.
notes.choices:
A) When the 10-year collection period ends
B) Only when he asks in writing
C) Within 30 days of full payment
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: section 6325(a) directs release within 30 days; a written request is for when that has not happened. C is wrong: full payment triggers release.
notes.explanation: Publication 1450 says section 6325(a) directs release within 30 days of full payment.
notes.source: Publication 1450, Instructions for Requesting a Certificate of Release of Federal Tax Lien (Rev. 7-2018), “Instructions for Requesting a Certificate of Release of Federal Tax Lien”, p. 1
notes.evidence: directs us to release a Federal tax lien within 30 days of when the liability is fully paid or becomes legally unenforceable, or the IRS accepts a bond for payment of the liability.

notes.front: A client wants to refinance his home mortgage, but the new lender will not lend while the federal tax lien has priority. What should he request?
notes.back: A: subordination of the federal tax lien to the new mortgage.
notes.choices:
A) Subordination
B) A certificate of discharge
C) A certificate of release
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: discharge removes property from the lien, typically on a sale. C is wrong: release needs the liability to be satisfied.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 gives refinancing a home mortgage as its example of subordination.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “How to make the Federal Tax Lien secondary to other creditors (“subordination”)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: refinance a mortgage on your home, but aren’t able to because the

notes.front: Release, withdrawal, discharge, subordination: which one clears both the lien and the public notice?
notes.back: Release. Withdrawal removes only the public notice, discharge frees one property and subordination changes priority.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 defines a release as clearing both the lien for the debt and the public Notice of Federal Tax Lien.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Understanding collection actions”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A “release” of a Federal Tax Lien means that we have cleared both

notes.front: How long before a levy must the IRS give written notice of its intention to levy?
notes.back: No less than 30 days before the day of the levy.
notes.explanation: Section 6331(d) lets the notice be given in person, left at the home or business, or sent by certified or registered mail.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6331, Levy and distraint, “(d) Requirement of notice before levy”
notes.evidence: no less than 30 days before the day of the levy.

notes.front: What are two situations where the IRS may levy without first offering a CDP hearing?
notes.back: Jeopardy; a levy on a state tax refund (also a federal contractor levy or a disqualified employment tax levy).
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the taxpayer then gets a letter explaining the seizure and appeal rights after the levy.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Reasons we may seize (“levy”) your property or rights to property”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A levy is served to collect tax from a state tax refund

notes.front: Must the IRS serve a new levy on each pay day to reach a taxpayer’s wages?
notes.back: No. One levy is served and continues until the debt is paid, other arrangements are made, the collection period ends or it is released.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 describes a wage levy as continuing rather than one-off.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Examples of property we can seize (“levy”)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: we will serve a levy once, not each time

notes.front: After receiving an IRS levy, how long does a bank hold the funds before sending them?
notes.back: 21 days, to allow disputes about who owns the account to be resolved.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the bank then sends the money with any interest earned on it.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Examples of property we can seize (“levy”)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: funds and give you 21 days to resolve any disputes about who

notes.front: What are two kinds of income that are exempt from IRS levy?
notes.back: Unemployment benefits; certain annuity and pension benefits (among others).
notes.explanation: Publication 594 also lists certain disability payments, workers’ compensation and court-ordered child support income, among others.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Property that can’t be seized (“levied”)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: the following: unemployment benefits, certain annuity and pension

notes.front: Within how long after a sale can a taxpayer recover seized real estate by repaying the purchaser?
notes.back: 180 days, paying the purchaser’s price plus interest.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 sets the interest at 20% a year, compounded daily.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “How to recover seized (“levied”) property that’s been sold”, p. 7
notes.evidence: may recoup it within 180 days of the sale by paying the purchaser

notes.front: Your client’s bank received an IRS levy yesterday. His business partner says half the money in the account is hers. What is the timing?
notes.back: A: the bank holds the funds for 21 days so the ownership dispute can be resolved.
notes.choices:
A) The bank holds the funds for 21 days
B) The bank must pay the IRS at once
C) The levy covers only deposits made after it is served
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the bank holds the funds first. C is wrong: the levy reaches funds available for withdrawal, up to the levy amount, when it is served.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 gives a 21-day window for disputes about who owns the account.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Examples of property we can seize (“levy”)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: funds and give you 21 days to resolve any disputes about who

notes.front: How long after a notice of intent to levy does a taxpayer have to request a CDP hearing?
notes.back: 30 days from the date of the notice.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the request goes to the address on the notice, using Form 12153.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “How to appeal a proposed seizure (“levy”)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You can request a Collection Due Process hearing within 30 days

notes.front: Which form is used to request a CDP hearing?
notes.back: Form 12153, Request for a Collection Due Process or Equivalent Hearing (or a written request with the same information).
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says it is sent to the address on the notice, not the payment address.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Collection Due Process”, p. 4
notes.evidence: To request a Collection Due Process hearing, complete Form 12153

notes.front: How many CDP levy hearings is a person entitled to for the same tax period?
notes.back: One.
notes.explanation: Section 6330(b)(2) allows one hearing per taxable period; Publication 1660 adds that a separate lien hearing is also available.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6330, Notice and opportunity for hearing before levy, “(b)(2) One hearing per period”
notes.evidence: A person shall be entitled to only one hearing under this section with respect to the taxable period

notes.front: What are two issues a taxpayer may raise at a CDP hearing?
notes.back: Any two of: spousal defences; the appropriateness of collection actions; collection alternatives such as an installment agreement or offer in compromise.
notes.explanation: Section 6330(c)(2)(A) lists these as examples of relevant issues relating to the unpaid tax or proposed levy.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6330, Notice and opportunity for hearing before levy, “(c)(2) Issues at hearing”
notes.evidence: (i) appropriate spousal defenses; (ii) challenges to the appropriateness of collection actions; and (iii) offers of collection alternatives

notes.front: When may a taxpayer challenge the existence or amount of the underlying tax at a CDP hearing?
notes.back: Only if the taxpayer did not receive the statutory deficiency notice for it or otherwise had no chance to dispute it.
notes.explanation: Section 6330(c)(2)(B) limits liability challenges to taxpayers who had no earlier opportunity.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6330, Notice and opportunity for hearing before levy, “(c)(2)(B) Underlying liability”
notes.evidence: if the person did not receive any statutory notice of deficiency for such tax liability or did not otherwise have an opportunity to dispute such tax liability.

notes.front: Within how many days of a CDP determination may the taxpayer petition the Tax Court?
notes.back: 30 days.
notes.explanation: Section 6330(d)(1) gives the Tax Court jurisdiction over the review.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6330, Notice and opportunity for hearing before levy, “(d)(1) Petition for review by Tax Court”
notes.evidence: The person may, within 30 days of a determination under this section, petition the Tax Court for review of such determination

notes.front: At a CDP hearing a client proposes only an installment agreement. After the determination, she wants the Tax Court to consider a spousal defence she never raised. What is the risk?
notes.back: C: she may not be able to raise it, because it was not raised with Appeals.
notes.choices:
A) None, if she petitions within 90 days
B) None: the Tax Court hears every issue afresh
C) She may be barred because she did not raise it at the hearing
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: issues not raised at the hearing may be lost. C is wrong: the petition deadline is 30 days, and timing does not cure the omission.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 warns that issues not raised during the Appeals hearing may not be raised in the Tax Court.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “What will happen when you request a CDP or equivalent hearing”, p. 2
notes.evidence: raise issues in the Tax Court if you do not raise them during the

notes.front: Can the IRS levy for the tax and periods covered while a timely CDP levy hearing is pending?
notes.back: No, unless an exception such as jeopardy applies; levy is barred for 30 days after the notice and during the hearing.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 names the section 6330(f) exceptions: jeopardy, state refunds, federal contractors and disqualified employment tax levies.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “What will happen when you request a CDP or equivalent hearing”, p. 2
notes.evidence: action is not permitted for the subject tax and periods during the

notes.front: What happens to the 10-year collection period during a timely CDP hearing?
notes.back: It is suspended until Appeals’ determination becomes final or the request is withdrawn.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 contrasts this with an equivalent hearing, which does not suspend it.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “What will happen when you request a CDP or equivalent hearing”, p. 2
notes.evidence: the IRS has to collect your taxes will be suspended until the

notes.front: By when must an equivalent hearing be requested after a missed CDP deadline?
notes.back: Within one year from the date of the notice.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 counts the lien version from one year plus 5 business days after the lien filing.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Collection Due Process”, p. 4
notes.evidence: not timely, you can request an Equivalent Hearing within one year from

notes.front: Compared with a timely CDP hearing, what two protections does an equivalent hearing lack?
notes.back: Levy is not prohibited, and the collection statute is not suspended (and there is no court review).
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 lists these as the consequences of an untimely request.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “What will happen when you request a CDP or equivalent hearing”, p. 2
notes.evidence: an equivalent hearing, the law does not prohibit levy and the

notes.front: A client received a Final Notice of Intent to Levy 18 days ago and wants to propose an installment agreement and keep the right to go to court. What do you file?
notes.back: B: Form 12153 requesting a CDP hearing, now.
notes.choices:
A) Form 12153 requesting an equivalent hearing
B) Form 12153 requesting a CDP hearing
C) Form 9423 under CAP
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: an equivalent hearing is for late requests and has no court review. C is wrong: CAP decisions cannot be taken to court.
notes.explanation: She is within 30 days of the notice, so a timely CDP request keeps Tax Court review and bars levy while it runs.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “How to appeal a proposed seizure (“levy”)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You can request a Collection Due Process hearing within 30 days

notes.front: A client first shows you a Final Notice of Intent to Levy dated 50 days ago. What hearing can he still ask for?
notes.back: C: an equivalent hearing, within one year of the notice.
notes.choices:
A) No hearing of any kind
B) A CDP hearing with Tax Court review
C) An equivalent hearing
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the 30-day CDP window has passed. C is wrong: an equivalent hearing is available for a year.
notes.explanation: Missing the CDP deadline leaves the one-year equivalent hearing, without court review.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Collection Due Process”, p. 4
notes.evidence: not timely, you can request an Equivalent Hearing within one year from

notes.front: At a CDP hearing a client wants to argue that the tax assessed is wrong. He received the statutory deficiency notice two years ago and ignored it. Can he raise the liability?
notes.back: C: no. He had a prior opportunity to dispute it.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, but only in writing
B) Yes, any issue may be raised at a CDP hearing
C) No, he had a prior opportunity to dispute it
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: section 6330(c)(2)(B) limits liability challenges. C is wrong: the form of the argument does not matter.
notes.explanation: Receiving the statutory notice counts as having had the chance to dispute the tax.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6330, Notice and opportunity for hearing before levy, “(c)(2)(B) Underlying liability”
notes.evidence: if the person did not receive any statutory notice of deficiency for such tax liability or did not otherwise have an opportunity to dispute such tax liability.

notes.front: Can a taxpayer go to court after a CAP decision they disagree with?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 gives this as the trade-off for CAP’s quicker and broader coverage.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “Collection Appeals Program”, p. 1
notes.evidence: However, you cannot go to court if you disagree with the CAP decision.

notes.front: Can a taxpayer dispute the amount of the tax owed in a CAP appeal?
notes.back: No. CAP cannot challenge the existence or amount of the liability.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 states this in contrast with CDP.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “Hearing available under Collection Appeals Program (CAP)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: challenge in CAP the existence or amount of your tax liability.

notes.front: Which installment agreement decisions can be appealed under CAP?
notes.back: Rejection, proposed or actual modification, and proposed or actual termination of an installment agreement.
notes.explanation: The Form 9423 instructions list installment agreement actions alongside liens, levies and seizures.
notes.source: Form 9423, Collection Appeal Request (Rev. 2-2020), “Instructions for Form 9423”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Rejected, proposed for modification or modified, or proposed for termination or terminated installment agreements.

notes.front: Besides the taxpayer, who may appeal a collection action under CAP?
notes.back: A third party whose property is subject to the collection action.
notes.explanation: The Form 9423 instructions open with this.
notes.source: Form 9423, Collection Appeal Request (Rev. 2-2020), “Instructions for Form 9423”, p. 2
notes.evidence: A taxpayer, or third party whose property is subject to a collection action, may appeal the following actions under the Collection Appeals Program (CAP):

notes.front: Before filing Form 9423 about a lien, levy or seizure, what must the taxpayer do first?
notes.back: Ask for a conference with the IRS employee’s manager.
notes.explanation: The Form 9423 instructions say Form 9423 follows only if the manager conference does not resolve the disagreement.
notes.source: Form 9423, Collection Appeal Request (Rev. 2-2020), “How to Appeal If You Disagree With a Lien, Levy, or Seizure Action”, p. 2
notes.evidence: If you disagree with the decision of the IRS employee, and wish to appeal, you must first request a conference with the employee's manager.

notes.front: After the conference with the Collection manager, within how many business days must Form 9423 be received or postmarked?
notes.back: 3 business days (after telling Collection within 2 business days that you will file).
notes.explanation: The instructions warn that collection action may resume if the deadline is missed.
notes.source: Form 9423, Collection Appeal Request (Rev. 2-2020), “How to Appeal If You Disagree With a Lien, Levy, or Seizure Action”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The Form 9423 must be received or postmarked within three (3) business days of the conference with the Collection manager or collection action may resume.

notes.front: What must a representative file to appear without the taxpayer at a CDP or CAP proceeding?
notes.back: A properly completed Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 says Form 8821 lets someone receive confidential material but not represent the taxpayer.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “Collection Appeal Rights”, p. 1
notes.evidence: If you want your representative to contact us or appear without you and to receive and inspect confidential material, you must file a properly completed Form 2848

notes.front: CAP or CDP: which gives Tax Court review, and which covers more kinds of collection action?
notes.back: CDP gives Tax Court review; CAP covers a broader range of actions (and is quicker) but has no court review.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 sets the two procedures side by side on these points.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “Collection Appeal Rights”, p. 1
notes.evidence: CAP generally results in a quicker Appeals decision and is available for a broader range of collection actions. However, you cannot go to court if you disagree with the CAP decision.

notes.front: The IRS has proposed to terminate a client’s installment agreement. No lien or levy notice has been issued. Which appeal route fits?
notes.back: C: the Collection Appeals Program.
notes.choices:
A) Tax Court petition
B) Collection Due Process
C) Collection Appeals Program
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: CDP needs a lien or levy notice. C is wrong: there is no determination for the Tax Court to review.
notes.explanation: Publication 1660 lists termination or proposed termination of an installment agreement among CAP actions.
notes.source: Publication 1660, Collection Appeal Rights (Rev. 1-2020), “Collection Appeals Program”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Termination, or proposed termination, of an installment agreement

notes.front: The IRS levied a car that belongs to your client, not to the taxpayer who owes the tax. Which procedure is open to your client?
notes.back: C: CAP, as a third party whose property is subject to collection.
notes.choices:
A) An equivalent hearing
B) A CDP hearing
C) CAP, as a third party
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: CDP and equivalent hearings follow notices issued to the taxpayer who owes the tax.
notes.explanation: Form 9423 lets a third party whose property is subject to a collection action appeal under CAP.
notes.source: Form 9423, Collection Appeal Request (Rev. 2-2020), “Instructions for Form 9423”, p. 2
notes.evidence: A taxpayer, or third party whose property is subject to a collection action, may appeal the following actions under the Collection Appeals Program (CAP):

notes.front: What are two debts other than federal tax that can be paid by offsetting a federal refund?
notes.back: Child support; certain federal non-tax debts such as student loans (also state income tax and spousal support, among others).
notes.explanation: The Form 1040 instructions list these; offsets other than for federal tax are made by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 (2025), “Refund Offset”, p. 61
notes.evidence: If you owe past-due federal tax, state income tax, state unemployment compensation debts, child support, spousal support, or certain federal nontax debts, such as student loans

notes.front: A client with overdue student loans and no federal tax debt receives a notice that his refund was reduced. Who sent the notice?
notes.back: C: the Bureau of the Fiscal Service.
notes.choices:
A) The Taxpayer Advocate Service
B) The IRS
C) The Bureau of the Fiscal Service
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the IRS sends notices only for federal tax offsets. C is wrong: the Taxpayer Advocate Service does not make offsets.
notes.explanation: Non-tax offsets are made, and notified, by the Fiscal Service.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 (2025), “Refund Offset”, p. 61
notes.evidence: For all other offsets, you will receive a notice from the Fiscal Service.

notes.front: Can Form 843 be used to amend a previously filed income tax return?
notes.back: No. Form 843 is not used to amend income or employment tax returns.
notes.explanation: The Form 843 instructions say not to use it when another tax form must be used.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 843 (Rev. December 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Also, do not use Form 843 to amend a previously filed income or employment tax return.

notes.front: A client wants the IRS to remove a penalty already assessed on her account. A second client wants to add a missed deduction to last year’s Form 1040. Which one uses Form 843?
notes.back: C: the penalty request; the deduction needs Form 1040-X.
notes.choices:
A) Both
B) The missed deduction
C) The penalty request
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: Form 843 is not used to amend an income tax return.
notes.explanation: Form 843 covers abatement of penalties; changes to an income tax return go on the amended return.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 843 (Rev. December 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Use Form 843 to claim a refund or request an abatement of certain taxes, penalties, additions to tax, interest, and fees.

notes.front: A client needs to amend three tax years. How many Forms 1040-X are filed?
notes.back: Three: a separate Form 1040-X for each year.
notes.explanation: The Form 1040-X instructions require one form per year amended.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040-X (Rev. December 2025), “General Instructions”, p. 2
notes.evidence: File a separate Form 1040-X for each year you are amending.

notes.front: Generally, by when must a claim for credit or refund be filed?
notes.back: Within 3 years from filing the original return or 2 years from paying the tax, whichever is later.
notes.explanation: The Form 843 instructions warn that a late claim may lose the right to the credit or refund.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 843 (Rev. December 2024), “Line 3”, p. 3
notes.evidence: you must file a claim for a credit or refund within 3 CAUTION years from the date you filed your original return or 2 years from

notes.front: A client filed her 2022 return on 10 April 2023 and paid all the tax then. On 20 May 2026 she finds a missed deduction. Can she still claim a refund?
notes.back: A: no. Both the 3-year and 2-year periods have ended.
notes.choices:
A) No, both periods have ended
B) Yes, she has 6 years
C) Yes, 3 years run from the 2023 due date plus extensions she did not ask for
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the general rule is 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment. C is wrong: no extension was requested, so none is added.
notes.explanation: The Form 1040-X instructions treat a return filed early as filed on the due date, 18 April 2023, so the 3 years ended on 18 April 2026; 2 years from payment ended in April 2025.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 843 (Rev. December 2024), “Line 3”, p. 3
notes.evidence: you must file a claim for a credit or refund within 3 CAUTION years from the date you filed your original return or 2 years from

notes.front: Can a taxpayer who did not appear for the audit later request audit reconsideration?
notes.back: Yes. Not appearing for the audit is one of the listed reasons.
notes.explanation: Publication 3598 also lists moving and not receiving IRS letters, and having new information.
notes.source: Publication 3598, The Audit Reconsideration Process (Rev. 11-2023), “Reasons for a Request”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Did not appear for your audit

notes.front: What must the documentation for an audit reconsideration request be?
notes.back: New information not presented before, for the tax year in question.
notes.explanation: Publication 3598 asks the taxpayer to check that the supporting documents are new.
notes.source: Publication 3598, The Audit Reconsideration Process (Rev. 11-2023), “Reasons for a Request”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Verify that the supporting documentation is new

notes.front: Which signed agreement with the IRS stops it accepting an audit reconsideration request?
notes.back: Form 906, Closing Agreement (a compromise agreement does too).
notes.explanation: Publication 3598 refuses reconsideration where the taxpayer has already agreed the tax in one of these ways.
notes.source: Publication 3598, The Audit Reconsideration Process (Rev. 11-2023), “The IRS will not accept your audit reconsideration request if”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Form 906, Closing Agreement; a Compromise

notes.front: Audit reconsideration can be requested anytime after an examination assessment, as long as the tax {{c1::remains unpaid}}.
notes.back: Remains unpaid.
notes.explanation: Publication 3598 sends taxpayers who have paid in full to a formal claim instead.
notes.source: Publication 3598, The Audit Reconsideration Process (Rev. 11-2023), “Frequently Asked Questions”, p. 2
notes.evidence: anytime after an examination assessment has been

notes.front: A client paid the audit assessment in full and now has new receipts. What should she file?
notes.back: A formal claim for refund on Form 1040-X, not an audit reconsideration request.
notes.explanation: Publication 3598 notes that full payment moves the dispute to a formal claim.
notes.source: Publication 3598, The Audit Reconsideration Process (Rev. 11-2023), “Reasons for a Request”, p. 1
notes.evidence: must file a formal claim (Form 1040X, Amended U.S.

notes.front: A client moved house, never saw the audit letters, and now owes an unpaid assessment. He has receipts that support his deductions. What should you request?
notes.back: B: audit reconsideration, with the new documentation.
notes.choices:
A) A CDP hearing
B) Audit reconsideration
C) Form 843 abatement of the tax
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: there is no lien or levy notice to appeal. C is wrong: Form 843 does not replace re-examining an audit adjustment to income tax.
notes.explanation: Publication 3598 lists moving and not receiving IRS correspondence, and having new information, as reasons to ask.
notes.source: Publication 3598, The Audit Reconsideration Process (Rev. 11-2023), “Reasons for a Request”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Have additional information to present that you

notes.front: Who is the personal representative of a decedent’s estate?
notes.back: An executor, administrator or anyone in charge of the decedent’s property.
notes.explanation: Publication 559 adds that an executor is usually named in the will to administer the estate.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Personal Representative”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A personal representative of an estate is an executor, administrator, or anyone who is in charge of the decedent's property.

notes.front: Which form tells the IRS that someone has been appointed to act as a fiduciary?
notes.back: Form 56.
notes.explanation: Publication 559 says a personal representative is a fiduciary and must give the IRS this written notice.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Form 56”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If you are appointed to act in a fiduciary capacity for another, you must file a written notice with the IRS stating this. Form 56 is used for this purpose.

notes.front: Is the decedent’s power of attorney acceptable evidence of appointment as personal representative?
notes.back: No. Neither a power of attorney nor a copy of the will is acceptable; the court certificate is.
notes.explanation: Publication 559 asks for a copy of the court certificate of appointment.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Claiming a refund”, p. 12
notes.evidence: (A power of attorney or a copy of the decedent's will isn't acceptable evidence of your appointment as the personal representative.)

notes.front: A court appointed your client as personal representative of his late father’s estate. The father’s final return shows a refund. What should be attached to the return?
notes.back: B: a copy of the court certificate of appointment.
notes.choices:
A) The father’s signed power of attorney
B) A copy of the court certificate of appointment
C) A copy of the will
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: Publication 559 says neither is acceptable evidence of appointment.
notes.explanation: With the certificate attached to the original return, Form 1310 is not needed.
notes.source: Publication 559 (2025), Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, “Claiming a refund”, p. 12
notes.evidence: file the return and attach a copy of the certificate that shows your appointment by the court.

notes.front: Whom may the IRS summon under section 7602(a)(2)?
notes.back: The person liable for tax, its officers or employees, anyone holding its books of account, or any other person the IRS deems proper.
notes.explanation: Section 7602(a)(2) reaches third parties such as record keepers, not only the taxpayer.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7602, Examination of books and witnesses, “(a) Authority to summon, etc.”
notes.evidence: To summon the person liable for tax or required to perform the act, or any officer or employee of such person

notes.front: By when may a taxpayer petition to quash a third-party summons issued to determine their liability?
notes.back: Before the end of the 20th day after the day notice is given.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the IRS will not review the third party’s information until the end of the 23rd day.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Summons: Used to secure information”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Petition to reject (“quash”) the summons before the end of the 20th

notes.front: Does a taxpayer get notice of a third-party summons issued to collect tax already owed?
notes.back: No, and the taxpayer cannot petition to quash it or intervene.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 distinguishes collection summonses from those used to determine liability.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Summons: Used to secure information”, p. 7
