notes.evidence: you won’t receive notice or be able to petition to reject or intervene in a suit to enforce the summons.

notes.front: While examining a client’s liability, the IRS summoned her bank’s records and notified her. She believes the summons is improper. What can she do?
notes.back: A: petition to quash it before the end of the 20th day after notice.
notes.choices:
A) Petition to quash it within 20 days of notice
B) Nothing: third-party summonses cannot be challenged
C) Ask for a CDP hearing
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a summons to determine liability can be challenged. C is wrong: CDP concerns lien and levy notices.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 gives the taxpayer the right to petition to quash a third-party summons used to determine liability.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Summons: Used to secure information”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Petition to reject (“quash”) the summons before the end of the 20th

notes.front: How long after assessment may the IRS collect tax by levy or court proceeding?
notes.back: Generally 10 years after the assessment.
notes.explanation: Section 6502(a) allows longer only in listed cases, such as a period agreed in writing with an installment agreement.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6502, Collection after assessment, “(a) Length of period”
notes.evidence: within 10 years after the assessment of the tax

notes.front: In bankruptcy, for how long is the collection period suspended?
notes.back: For the time collection is barred by the automatic stay, plus 6 months.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 lists bankruptcy among the suspension events.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “How long we have to collect taxes”, p. 4
notes.evidence: can’t collect because of the automatic stay, plus 6 months.

notes.front: Tax was assessed on 1 June 2015. Nothing has suspended or extended the collection period and no court case was brought. Can the IRS begin a levy in 2026?
notes.back: B: no. The 10-year period ended on 1 June 2025.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the IRS has 15 years
B) No, the 10-year period ended in 2025
C) Yes, the period runs from the return’s due date
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the period is 10 years. C is wrong: section 6502 counts from assessment.
notes.explanation: Section 6502(a) allows levy only within 10 years after assessment unless an exception applies.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6502, Collection after assessment, “(a) Length of period”
notes.evidence: within 10 years after the assessment of the tax

notes.front: Under section 6672, how large is the trust fund recovery penalty?
notes.back: Equal to the total tax not collected, or not accounted for and paid over.
notes.explanation: Publication 15 describes the same rule as 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax, not a percentage of it.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6672, Failure to collect and pay over tax, “(a) General rule”
notes.evidence: be liable to a penalty equal to the total amount of the tax evaded, or not collected, or not accounted for and paid over.

notes.front: The trust fund recovery penalty is {{c1::100%}} of the unpaid trust fund tax.
notes.explanation: Publication 15 states the rate this way in its deposit penalty section.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2026), Employer's Tax Guide, “Trust fund recovery penalty”, p. 36
notes.evidence: The penalty is 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax.

notes.front: Which taxes are trust fund taxes?
notes.back: The income tax, social security tax and Medicare tax withheld from employees’ wages.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the employer holds these “in trust” for the government until deposited.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “About trust fund taxes”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Trust fund taxes are the income tax, Social Security tax, and Medicare

notes.front: Besides being a responsible person, what state of mind does section 6672 require for the TFRP?
notes.back: Wilfulness: the person wilfully failed to collect, account for or pay over the tax.
notes.explanation: Section 6672(a) imposes the penalty only on a person who acts wilfully.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6672, Failure to collect and pay over tax, “(a) General rule”
notes.evidence: who willfully fails to collect such tax, or truthfully account for and pay over such tax

notes.front: After Letter 1153 proposes a TFRP, how long does the person have to appeal if the disagreement is not resolved?
notes.back: 60 days from the date of the letter.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 points to Publication 5 for how to prepare the appeal.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Trust Fund Recovery Penalty”, p. 8
notes.evidence: If you can’t resolve the disagreement with us, you have 60 days from the date of the Letter 1153 to appeal with Appeals.

notes.front: Can the TFRP be assessed after the company has gone out of business?
notes.back: Yes, regardless of whether the company is still in business.
notes.explanation: Publication 594 says the penalty is assessed against the responsible person personally.
notes.source: Publication 594, The IRS Collection Process (Rev. 1-2026), “Trust Fund Recovery Penalty”, p. 8
notes.evidence: We may assess this penalty against a responsible person regardless of whether the company is still in business.

notes.front: A company’s finance manager signs all cheques. Knowing that payroll withholding is overdue, she pays suppliers first to keep the business going. Is she exposed to the TFRP?
notes.back: C: yes. She is a responsible person who acted wilfully.
notes.choices:
A) No, because she did not keep the money herself
B) No, only the company’s owner can be liable
C) Yes, a responsible person acting wilfully
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: officers and employees can be responsible persons. C is wrong: section 6672 asks whether she wilfully failed to pay over the tax, not whether she benefited.
notes.explanation: She had the duty to pay over the tax and knowingly chose other creditors.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6672, Failure to collect and pay over tax, “(a) General rule”
notes.evidence: who willfully fails to collect such tax, or truthfully account for and pay over such tax

notes.front: A business withheld $40,000 of income, social security and Medicare tax from staff and never deposited it. What is the maximum TFRP?
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: the penalty is 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax, not a percentage of it.
notes.explanation: The TFRP equals the whole unpaid trust fund tax.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2026), Employer's Tax Guide, “Trust fund recovery penalty”, p. 36
notes.evidence: The penalty is 100% of the unpaid trust fund tax.

notes.front: What was the seriously delinquent tax debt threshold for 2025?
notes.explanation: The IRS table adjusts the figure yearly for inflation; the exam window tests 2025.
notes.source: IRS, “Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes”, “What are seriously delinquent tax debts?”

notes.front: Besides the amount, what collection step must have happened for a debt to be seriously delinquent?
notes.back: An NFTL filed with administrative remedies lapsed or exhausted, or a levy issued.
notes.explanation: The IRS page states these alternatives.
notes.source: IRS, “Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes”, “What are seriously delinquent tax debts?”
notes.evidence: The IRS must have filed a Notice of Federal Tax Lien, and all administrative remedies under the law have lapsed or been exhausted, or the IRS must have issued a levy

notes.front: A debt is being timely paid under an approved installment agreement. Can it be certified as seriously delinquent?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The IRS page lists this exclusion alongside debts being timely paid under an accepted offer in compromise.
notes.source: IRS, “Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes”, “What tax debts aren’t certified to the State Department?”
notes.evidence: Debts being timely paid through approved installment agreements,

notes.front: Will the IRS certify a taxpayer whose account is currently not collectible for hardship?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The IRS page also excludes identity theft victims, taxpayers in bankruptcy and those in disaster areas, among others.
notes.source: IRS, “Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes”, “What tax debts aren’t certified to the State Department?”
notes.evidence: Has an account that's been determined to be “currently not collectible” due to hardship,

notes.front: Does paying a certified debt down below the threshold reverse the certification?
notes.back: No. The certified debt must be fully resolved; partial payments below the threshold are not enough.
notes.explanation: The IRS page reverses certification when the debt is fully satisfied, becomes unenforceable, is no longer seriously delinquent or was certified in error.
notes.source: IRS, “Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes”, “Reversal of certification”
notes.evidence: the IRS will not reverse the certification if the debt becomes lower than the threshold amount through partial payments or collection statute expirations.

notes.front: In 2025 a client owes $70,000 of assessed income tax. An NFTL was filed, his appeal rights have run out and he has no payment plan. What is his passport risk?
notes.back: C: the IRS may certify the debt, and the State Department may deny or revoke his passport.
notes.choices:
A) None, as long as he has not travelled abroad
B) None: only debts over $100,000 count
C) The debt may be certified to the State Department
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the 2025 threshold was $64,000. C is wrong: certification does not depend on travel.
notes.explanation: He is over the 2025 threshold and meets the lien condition, with no exclusion such as an installment agreement.
notes.source: IRS, “Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes”, “What are seriously delinquent tax debts?”
notes.evidence: Generally, the State Department will not issue passports to taxpayers after receiving their delinquent debt certification from the IRS.
